steps.text: Most lost pieces were not outplayed by a clever trick. They were left where something could simply take them. [I] Seeing which squares a piece reaches is how you spot that, for you and for your opponent.

You just moved the rook. Now a new word. A piece **attacks** a square if it would be able to capture an enemy piece standing there, as far as the board is concerned. Whether the capture is also safe, or legal for your king, is a separate question. The square can be empty for now. If a piece of your own side stands on it, your piece **defends** it. Not sure yet? The next board shows a worked example before you answer anything.

steps.caption: White to move. The lit squares are every square the rook attacks. The black pawn on d7 is one of them.

line.say: The rook attacks d7, so it may capture the pawn there. The square d8 behind the pawn was never attacked.

claims.statement: The rook attacks exactly these 13 squares.
A black pawn stands on d7.
The rook can capture the pawn on d7.

steps.text: **A line stops at the first piece.** A rook, bishop or queen cannot jump over another piece, so whatever stands first blocks the line. These pieces attack every square along a line, up to and including the first piece they meet. If that piece is an enemy, it is attacked. If it is a friend, it is defended. The squares behind it are not attacked at all.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on d6 shields the black rook on d8: the white rook's line ends at d6.

claims.statement: The rook attacks d5 and d6 upward, but not d8.
The rook attacks the pawn on d6.
No white piece attacks the rook on d8.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rook on d4 stands behind its own pawn on d6, so the rook defends the pawn.

line.say: The bishop captures the pawn on d6, because the pawn is attacked.
The rook was defending d6, so it can capture the bishop at once.

claims.statement: The rook defends the pawn on d6.
The bishop attacks d6.
The rook defends d6.
The bishop can capture the pawn.

steps.text: **Attacked and defended are separate facts.** A piece can be both at once, like the bishop in the last question. If the attacker takes, the defender can take back, so the attacker has to ask what it wins and what it loses. On the earlier rook board the rook took back, so the bishop's capture lost a bishop for a pawn. Attacked and defended is only the start of the count; later lessons teach the count. [I] These are ideas from this lesson, not a law.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop's diagonal toward the black side ends at the pawn on f6.

line.say: The bishop captures on f6. The squares g7 and h8 behind the pawn were not attacked.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks exactly these nine squares, ending at f6.
The bishop can capture the pawn on f6.
The square g7 behind the pawn is not attacked.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen moves like a rook and a bishop together, so eight lines leave it. Each ends at the first piece it meets.

claims.statement: The queen attacks exactly these 23 squares.
A black pawn stands on d7.
A black knight stands on g7.
A black bishop stands on a7.
A white pawn stands on b4.
A white pawn stands on f2.

steps.text: **Walk each direction.** Start at the piece. Take one direction at a time and stop at the first piece: an enemy there is attacked, a friend there is defended. Then turn to the next direction. The next boards show this routine on an opening position.

steps.caption: White's rook on e1, direction one: up the e-file. It reaches the black knight on e4 and stops. The pawn on e5 behind the knight is not attacked. Direction four, down: the rook is already on the first row, so there is nothing below.

claims.statement: The rook attacks exactly d1, f1, g1, e2, e3 and e4.
A black knight stands on e4.
The rook does not attack e5, behind the knight.

steps.caption: Direction two: left along the first row. The rook meets its own queen on d1 at once and stops, so it defends the queen.

claims.statement: The rook attacks exactly d1, f1, g1, e2, e3 and e4.
The white queen stands on d1.
The rook does not attack c1, behind the queen.

steps.caption: Direction three: right along the first row. f1 is empty, then the white king stands on g1. The rook defends the king's square and goes no further.

claims.statement: The rook attacks exactly d1, f1, g1, e2, e3 and e4.
The white king stands on g1.
The rook does not attack h1, behind the king.

steps.title: Same bishop, three boards
steps.prompt: White bishop on b2, black knight on f6, in three positions. Which of them has the bishop attacking the knight? Predict for each, then check.

steps.text: **Knights jump.** A knight attacks the squares a knight's move away, and nothing in between can block it: pieces of either colour may stand all around it. From the middle of the board it attacks eight squares. From a corner it attacks only two.

steps.caption: A knight in the middle of an empty board attacks eight squares.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 attacks exactly eight squares.

steps.caption: The same knight in the corner attacks only two squares, f2 and g3; in the middle it attacked eight. [I] With fewer squares to reach, a knight in the corner has fewer things it can do.

claims.statement: The knight on h1 attacks only f2 and g3.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight on f3 jumps over White's own pawns, and it attacks the black pawn on e5. No black piece defends that pawn yet.

line.say: Black develops the knight to c6, where it defends the pawn on e5.

claims.statement: The knight on f3 attacks exactly eight squares, including its own pieces on d2, e1 and h2.
The knight attacks e5.
No black piece defends e5 yet.
After the move the knight on c6 defends e5.

steps.text: **Pawns are odd.** A pawn moves straight ahead but attacks the two squares diagonally ahead of it. It attacks them even when they are empty, and even when the pawn itself is blocked. It never attacks the square straight in front. White pawns attack upward; Black pawns attack downward.

steps.caption: The pawn can move only to e5. But it attacks d5 and f5, two squares it cannot move to.

claims.statement: The pawn can move only to e5.
The pawn attacks d5 and f5, not e5.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn is blocked by the pawn on e5, but the bishop on f5 stands on a diagonal square.

line.say: The blocked pawn still captures diagonally, taking the bishop on f5.

claims.statement: The pawn attacks d5 and f5.
The blocked pawn's only legal move is the capture on f5.
The pawn can capture the bishop.

steps.caption: Black to move. A black pawn attacks downward, toward White: it attacks c4 and e4.

line.say: The black pawn captures the white knight on c4, one step diagonally down.

claims.statement: The pawn on d5 attacks c4 and e4.
The pawn can capture the knight.

steps.title: Same pawn, one change
steps.prompt: White pawn on d4, a black knight nearby, in three positions. Which of them has the pawn attacking the knight? Predict for each, then check.

steps.text: **The king attacks every square one step away,** up to eight squares. Like any piece, it defends friends standing on those squares. A king attacks all eight squares, but it still cannot step onto a square an enemy piece attacks. Later lessons explain why an attacked square matters so much to a king; for now, just learn to see the squares.

steps.caption: The king attacks the eight squares around it: its own pawn on d3 is defended, and the black pawn on e5 is attacked.

claims.statement: The king attacks exactly the eight squares around it.
A white pawn stands on d3.
A black pawn stands on e5.

steps.text: **Attacks are counted.** Look at a square and ask two questions: how many enemy pieces attack it, and how many of my pieces defend it? As a rule of thumb, more attackers than defenders is a reason to look closer, because captures happen in turns and every attacker needs an answer from a defender. It is not yet proof that a capture wins; later lessons teach the exact count.

steps.caption: Black to move. The pawn on f7 is attacked twice, by the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5, and defended once, by the king.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack f7.
One black piece defends f7.
The bishop attacks f7.
The knight attacks f7.

steps.caption: White to move. The black bishop on c5 attacks the pawn on f2; the white king defends it. One attacker, one defender: a square to keep an eye on.

claims.statement: One black piece attacks f2.
One white piece, the king, defends f2.
The bishop attacks f2.

steps.caption: White to move. Each rook attacks the other. Attacks work in both directions, and the player to move gets to capture first.

line.say: White captures first. No black piece can capture the rook on e8, so Black cannot take back.

claims.statement: The white rook attacks the black rook.
The black rook attacks the white rook.
The white rook can capture on e8.
After the capture no black piece attacks e8.

steps.text: **Check the last move.** Dan Heisman teaches that you should look at what your opponent's last move now attacks before choosing your own [S: see sources]. [H] Many beginner losses may come less from missing a clever trick than from skipping that look; we have no data on this, so test it on your own games.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks why the queen does not attack the square behind a pawn. Write two sentences to answer them, then compare with the checklist.

steps.text: **Compare with this checklist.** Did you say: a piece attacks a square if it could capture an enemy piece there, and a friend on the square is defended; rooks, bishops and queens stop at the first piece, so the squares behind it are not attacked; knights jump; pawns attack the two squares diagonally ahead, even when blocked; the king attacks one step around; a piece can be attacked and defended at once? Add whatever you missed in your own words.
